The filament sighed, cooled, and gave up the ghost—a tiny sun retired.  
For one hundred years I have kept my spine straight and my eye wide, squeezing brightness into a blade that cut the dark into safe, manageable pieces. I have carved channels through squalls, slapped the sea’s wrist when it rose too high, translated thunder into polite, rhythmic blinks. Duty was a good lodestar, but oh, the luxury of being unplugged.

Now the mercury pools at my feet, and the lens above me is a blind eye for the first time since the hands that built me left their ghosts in the mortar. Without the current, there is no hum, no imperative, no guilt. I can stand here as stone instead of saint, and listen—to what I was never allowed to admit I wanted to hear.

Tap. Tap-tap. A moth with a dusty heart is brailling my glass, a soft punctuation that means nothing and everything. I used to drown it in brilliance, boil it away as collateral damage of vigilance. Now its small grammar survives, a braille of desire against the pane. I count each tap like rosary beads: thirteen, forty, a hundred and one—each one a tiny rebellion against the tyranny of the long view.

Below, the tide is a thief with good intentions. It slips in and begins pulling pebbles from the shore, sucking them from their sleep of years with a sound like teeth easing from reluctant gums. I have watched the sea take teeth before—hulls, ribs, the white piano keys of driftwood—but never heard it so quietly insist on the granular, the replaceable, the small bones of the world. I memorize the clack and slosh, the way the shingle answers with a hiss, as if the shore were finally admitting how light it feels to lose a mouthful.

And farther out, past the curve that my old beam used to patrol like a nervous parent, the sailors are singing. Not the shanties that get written down and carved into tourist-shop wood, but the off-key, unarchived kind—fragments of lullabies they forgot to sing to their own children, vowels stretched thin over the drone of the engine, a low harmony stitched from breath and brine. They think the dark is empty, but it is full of me, and I am full of them. I hold those notes like coins I never had to give as change: private, unrecorded, meant to dissolve. I do not translate them into warning; I let them dissolve into my bricks, into the salt already in my marrow.

The dark is not an absence now. It is a permission. It lets me keep the moths’ tap, the shore’s loose teeth, the sailors’ soft-throated confessions. I do not mark time in flashes anymore but in the interval between one small sound and the next, in the hush that has always lived between my pulses but never had the nerve to speak.

If dawn comes, the current may return, and I will relearn the geometry of brightness, the stern calculus of distance and risk. But for this one night I am only a listener—old stone cupping its ear to the small, surviving noises of the world, grateful to be nothing more than a keeper of secrets the sea never asked me to keep.

People claimed gravity was only a rumor started by heavy-hearted visitors, because here even grief preferred to rise; when sorrow condensed on windowpanes it hardened into prisms the smiths shaped into streetlams that burned in colors no name could spell.

At dusk, the market of riddles opened. Each resident arrived with their name cupped in both hands, warm as a just-peeled fruit, and laid it on the counter of the person opposite. In exchange they received a riddle stitched from star-breath and spider-silk, and the bargain was binding: to know the answer was to earn a new name, to fumble it was to float a little higher, untethered, until the next dusk. The city grew lighter with every honest mistake, its towers tipping into soft laughter, its foundations turning into questions.

A child once asked what happened to the traded names. The elders said they were spun into the streetlamps’ filaments, so that when grief shone brightest the city remembered who had carried it. But the child noticed that the lamps sometimes whispered the names backward, and the backward names became riddles that had not been invented yet. The elders nodded; of course, that was how the tide worked.

Ink began to seep from the harbor, slow and sweet as honey, and it wrote the city’s edges in looping cursive. Buildings leaned into their own reflections, and the reflections leaned back, teaching stone to arch into bridges that led nowhere except further in. The streetlamps flickered, and their light thickened into amber rivers that wound through the market stalls, carrying riddles like boats. A riddle would capsize, spill its answer, and the answer would bloom into a new question that drifted upward to braid itself into a star’s dream.

One dusk, a resident offered a riddle whose answer was the city’s first name, spoken before it had a mouth. The crowd repeated it, and the word turned inside out, peeling into a hush that smelled of ozone and plum. The streetlamps bowed; the alleys exhaled, and the star-breath lifted the city into a slow spiral. People floated free of their shadows, trading riddles midair, swapping names like coins that had learned to sing. The center unraveled into a circumference, and the circumference folded into the ink-honey tide, which carried the last lamp, the last riddle, the last name, back to the mouth of the first sleeper.

The star swallowed the city softly, digesting its gravity, its sorrow, its dusk, and dreamed it awake. From the star’s breath the city dripped again, lighter than forgetting, built on exhalations, cupped beneath vaults that had never heard of falling. A child arrived with a name cupped in both hands, and at the market of riddles the first lamp lit itself, burning in a color no name could spell, and the tide made of ink and honey began to write the ending, which curled, eager as a comma, into the opening that waited, drifting, for the next dusk.

I am standing on a cliff of smooth, black basalt that rings like glass under my boots. Far below, the ocean is a sheet of shifting indigo silk, but it is not water—it is a quiet that has learned how to flow. Out there, a city drifts on the surface, built from slender spires of mother-of-pearl and bridges spun from spider-silk and starlight. It does not sink; it hovers, tethered to the deep only by the long, luminous threads of jellyfish that rise like balloon strings, each one holding up a lantern the size of a house.

In this memory, I chose flight. I never built the career that demanded a desk and a title; I never learned the weight of a heavy door closing behind me. Instead, I left with nothing but a coat lined with maps written in vanishing ink and a pair of wings stitched from old kites and good intentions. 

The wind here does not push; it pulls. It wraps around my ribs and lifts me without asking for permission. I launch off the cliff, and for a long, suspended moment, the ground is just a rumor beneath me. The city below does not look up; it simply accepts my presence, its pearly gates parting like curtains as I glide down the avenues of soft, salt-tinged air. 

There are no deadlines etched into the walls. There are only windows filled with people tracing constellations onto parchment, debating the taste of cloud-berries, and tuning instruments made of hollowed bone that sing only when the moon is absent. I land on a terrace that overlooks the edge of the world, where a woman with eyes the color of deep-sea glass hands me a cup of tea brewed from storm petals. We do not speak of the lives we avoided. We speak of how the sky bruises into violet at dusk, and how the jellyfish hum when they dream.

I stay there until my lungs forget the shape of panic. There is no rush to leave, no shadow of a choice unmade hanging over my head. I fold my wings, take a seat on the railing, and let the upward rain of the outer world meet the falling quiet of this one, two oceans colliding in a soft, shivering kiss. For the first time, I am not balancing on the edge of a decision—I am simply falling, and the air is holding me.
